text: In Anthropic's own internal research evaluation, its multi-agent research system substantially outperformed a single-agent Claude Opus 4 baseline.
Most of the performance gain of multi-agent research systems is explained by greater token/compute spend rather than by agent structure per se.
At matched inference cost or token budget, multi-agent research/reasoning systems do not reliably outperform a single well-prompted agent.
On deep-research report benchmarks (e.g., DeepResearch Bench), dedicated deep-research agents score higher than LLMs given only search tools.
On difficult ML research replication/engineering benchmarks (PaperBench, MLE-bench), autonomous agents still fall well short of human experts.
Giving the same model an agentic scaffold (iterative tool use / longer horizon) improves results on hard ML research tasks compared to a less agentic scaffold.

hypothesis: Across published same-model comparisons, more agentic/iterative scaffolds give large relative gains on hard ML research tasks, comparable in size to pure compute gains (pass@k, time)
result: Same-model scaffold gains 1.85-10.9x (PaperBench Iterative vs Basic 24.4 vs 13.2 for o1; MLE-bench AIDE vs OpenHands/MLAB 8.7 vs 4.4/0.8); compute-only gains similar magnitude (pass@8 vs pass@1 2.0x; 100h vs 24h 1.36x); equal-cost multi-agent vs single 1.02x (n.s.); best PaperBench agent reaches 0.63 of human baseline
